en: Take heed of what I say:
When slung, the mirror of one's shoulder,
When wielded against a clashing enemy,
The comfort of a life held in trust,
Ochogor when at play,
Koychagyr when in earnest,
Almabash, the finest iron,
Which makes no distinction between far and near,
When a life held in trust is hard pressed,
Does not fail for twelve days.
My khan, agree to what I say;
To your daughter's son who has sheltered in Bukhara,
Give the gray short gun!”
His grandmother cried out,
“Give the property as a gift!”
She kept saying through her sobs.
As soon as Khan Temir heard,
Surrounded by a garden of plane trees,
With a golden throne in the middle,
Though soaked in water forty years,
Not the slightest edge had faded;
Though soaked in water eight years,
It had not frayed or rotted.
From upon the golden throne,
From the surface of that carpet,
He ran in haste.
A tower stood at the foot of the throne;
He ran to the tower,
Climbed up and looked:
That orphan Semetey
Had put on the guise of Manas.
His wrath terrified souls;
A black-spotted leopard
Raged at his side.
A short-tailed, fierce lion
Stood ready beside him.
A banner fluttered in his hand;
The gray pouch-belt left by his father Manas
Gleamed about his mighty waist.
A cap of gray lynx and marten
He had put on his head, excited.
Royal Bukhara's city,
As though he would slaughter it all,
The boy stood in a frenzy.
The keen steel left by his father Manas
He had slung snugly upon his forearm.
The battle-axe with golden cheeks
He had taken from his poor mother Kanykey.
His bearing and appearance,
Each limb, his very shape,
Had become like his father Manas's.
The people who watched
Seemed to see that man running.
The enemy plainly seemed
To despair of life.
Leaving offspring behind,
Plainly the leopard Manas,
The man, seemed to have come alive.
To the plump, gray-mottled goshawk,
Her heart aching, unable to stand,
For the morning star left by her husband Manas,
With many worries in her heart,
For her foal, the child Kanykey had borne,
Raging and grieving,
With only a spoonful of blood left,
Her flesh reduced to gray lean meat,
Raging, coming straight ahead,
Aktulpar from the palace
His maternal grandfather, Khan Temir,
Led forth and offered as a gift.
Putting a belt about his neck,
Khan Temir stood lamenting,
Pleading with Semetey:
“Oh, Semetey, my foal,
If you wish to go to your father,
Many bear evil thoughts;
Many enemies await an encounter with you.
The Chinese are on your flank,
Guns are before you;
Many enemies stand ready to contend with you.
I taught it speech for the enemy;
Let me give you a companion from the mute beasts.
My foal, orphan Semetey,
Take my sword-snouted elephant,
My precious orphan, heed my words!
When hardship fell upon you,
My child, you were the one who fled here.
Contending with many lands,
When hardship fell upon you,
My child, I was the one who raised you.
Having ninety beasts slaughtered for your feast,
My child, having you treated differently,
Calling you the orphan left by the winged steed,
Calling you the plump, gray-mottled goshawk,
I raised you with care for your bearing, Semetey,
Calling you gray hawk, morning star.
This Bukhara here,
My dear orphan,
Let me drive it all together,
Gather every one of them,
My dear Semetey,
And set them in a long procession.
Choose a rendezvous at a measured place;
My dear foal,
Choose companions suited to you.
From marksmen who never miss,
My child, let me give you a hundred;
From skilled spearmen,
Let me give you a hundred;
From mighty battle-axe wielders,
Let me give you a hundred.
When a black gun cracks,
Those who stand and fight without fleeing,
Let me give you a hundred able men.
When a fearsome gun bangs,
Those who enter battle without fear,
My child, let me give you a hundred stalwarts.
From speakers born with swift tongues,
Let me give you a hundred!
From companions who stand by you till death,
Let me give you a hundred.
The reason I give a hundred of each—
Broad Talas is no land for you;
Abyke is no kin to you;
Your grandfather, that swine of a khan, is no father to you!
Let me tell you of your grandfather, that swine of a khan:
There will be evasions in his words,
There will be malice in his eyes;
If he can, he will seek to strike you down.
There will be crookedness in his words,
There will be a squint in his eyes;
If he finds his chance, my orphan,
He will do something to you.
Deceit lurks in his words,
Wickedness lurks in his eyes.
If you turn toward Talas,
My orphan, he seeks to ruin you.
There is something else in his words;
If they can, the six scoundrels
Seek to tear you apart.
Ride him on reconnaissance, he will not tire;
Ride him with the baggage train, he will not ail;
Ride him six months, he will not grow lean.
Unless his appointed death arrives,
However long he goes, he will not age.
A Karabayir racehorse,
Tireless lungs and brass forelegs,
Even when his lead rope is down to a handspan,
He will not yield to a determined foe.
Unless the true hour of death comes,
He will not let an enemy strike his rider.
Let me choose from the horses and give you one;
My foal, take my steed, one like Aktulpar.
If your companions are too few,
My foal, orphan, take my life;
Take my city of Bukhara,
Take all the brave men.
Leave my two and take my one;
Leave my file and take my whetstone.
How many words I have cried aloud!
Without killing me, orphan, heed my words.
Thinking, ‘My grandfather Khan Temir is unfortunate,’
Recognize this service of mine!
In a gunfight, no bullet will pierce it;
In a lance fight, no spear will pierce it.
Your grandfather chose and gave it;
I gave the blue padded coat: wear it as you go.
I gave Aktulpar: ride him as you go.
Then go to Talas,
Go and recite the Quran thus,
For your only father Manas, gone to the other world!”
When his grandfather Khan Temir had spoken so,
And, as he wished, had offered Aktulpar
As a gift to the orphan,
Overcome with joy,
He put on the unpierceable garment
Of his grandfather Temir.
Its front pommel of white gold,
Its rear bow of solid silver,
Its two sides of broad iron,
A broad-pommel saddle for mounted wrestling,
A little apprehensive,
The boy then saddled up
And mounted Aktulpar.
His grandfather Khan Temir's gray short gun
He now slung over his shoulder.
The gray pouch-belt left by his father Manas
He fastened snugly about his waist.
Smiling yet looking somber,
Radiance touched his sun-like face;
Staring wide-eyed yet looking somber,
Radiance touched his moon-like face.
At the sight, hearts were moved;
The fierce leopard Manas
Seemed to have come to life this very day.
Your boy wandered toward the people;
Upon the orphan left alone,
All the weapons and armor
Sat just as on his father Manas.
When they saw his appearance,
The people wept, the khan wept;
All the great throng wept.
The white-turbaned khoja wept;
The mullah who had studied his lessons wept.
The hard-hearted lord wept;
Even the charging warrior wept.
All those who wept,
Wept, consumed by their own grief.
For each brave young man,
For each and every one,
They wept, wishing a child might remain.
As the people stood grieving,
Semetey did something astonishing:
“My dear grandfather,
Who should hear these words of yours?
Let the night that blinds the eyes hear them,
Let the great dug pit hear them,
Let boiling misery hear them!
Who else should hear them?
Taking an iron-rope net,
Taking troops all around me,
How could I do such a thing?
The treasure left by my precious father,
How could I slaughter the Kyrgyz?
A lord's only child,
Setting out with troops from you,
Going to attack the Kyrgyz,
Would it be good to turn wicked?
‘Lay waste and attack the people,’ you say—
Father, are these good words of yours?
Can a khan's child prosper
By destroying a city?
‘Go and attack your own people,’ you say—
Grandfather, are these good words of yours?
Gathering troops from you,
How could I make my reconnaissance?
There is no Chinese enemy opposing me;
Against my kinsmen Abyke and Kobosh,
How could I go to fight?
Can a khan's only child
Prosper by assailing his people?
‘Choose warriors and take an army,’ you say—
Grandfather, is there a troublemaker like you?
When death comes, I shall die.
Saying ‘Amen!’ with hands spread,
For my father gone to the other world,
I shall go and recite the Quran!”
Raging, Semetey
Only half received
His grandfather Temir's blessing,
Not letting the slightest thought leave him
Of his father gone to the other world.
The mount beneath him
Was Khan Temir's winged steed;
What he held in his hand
Was Ismayyl's steel.
